package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware sample, not a versioned package)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire payload is designed to evade email security gateways using multi-layered archive nesting, ultimately delivering BazarBackdoor malware. This malware provides remote access to attackers, can download further payloads (such as Cobalt Strike), and is used for post-exploitation, lateral movement, and enabling ransomware or data theft.

execution_context.trigger: user-initiated (after extraction and double-clicking JavaScript file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user executes the JavaScript file, it launches the disguised .png payload (actually an executable), which initiates the BazarBackdoor malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: JavaScript files in email attachments that execute local files are a common malware delivery vector. The use of ActiveXObject and shell execution is a red flag.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal JavaScript files in archives should not execute binaries or interact with the filesystem in this way.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise deployment scripts may use similar techniques, but never as unsolicited email attachments.
key_indicators: Execution of a file with a misleading extension

execution_context.file_location: Extracted payload file (payload.png, actually an EXE)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the disguised executable establishes a connection to a command-and-control server, downloads and executes additional payloads (such as Cobalt Strike), and provides remote access to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: A file with a .png extension that is actually an executable is a classic malware obfuscation technique. The behavior of connecting to C2 and downloading further payloads is highly malicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A .png file should be an image, not an executable. Executables should not be disguised as images.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for executables disguised as images in user-facing archives.
key_indicators: File extension mismatch (image extension, executable content)

attack_chain.action: Phishing email delivers nested RAR/ZIP archive to user.
User extracts and opens JavaScript file from nested archive.
BazarBackdoor executable connects to C2, downloads further payloads (e.g., Cobalt Strike), and provides remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistence, can deploy ransomware or steal data.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript files in email archives that execute local files
Execution of files with misleading extensions (e.g., .png that is an EXE)
Unexpected network connections from newly executed binaries
Multi-layered archive extraction with mixed archive types
file_indicators: Nested .zip and .rar files in email attachments
Files with image extensions (.png) that are actually executables
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known BazarBackdoor C2 infrastructure
Subsequent connections to Cobalt Strike C2 servers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for email attachments containing nested archives with mixed types (ZIP, RAR). Flag JavaScript files within archives that attempt to execute local files or launch executables. Detect files with mismatched extensions (e.g., .png files that are actually Windows executables). Monitor for new processes making suspicious outbound network connections, especially shortly after archive extraction and script execution.
